en: Thus have I heard: Majjhima Nikāya 131, the Bhaddekaratta Sutta (The Discourse on One Fortunate Night) Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, I will teach you the summary and the exposition of ‘One Who Has Had a Single Fortunate Night.’”
“Listen to that and pay close attention; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“One should not pursue the past,
nor should one long for the future;
what is past has been relinquished.”
And that which has not yet been reached, the future;
and whatever phenomenon is present—
whosoever discerns them each in their respective place;
Unshakable and unassailable—
let the wise person cultivate that.
What must be done should be done with diligence this very day.
Who knows when death will come tomorrow?
For we have no agreement with that Death who possesses a great army.
One who dwells thus,
ardent and untiring by day and night,
is indeed called "Bhaddekaratta."
The sage, being virtuous, explains this.
And how, monks, does one pursue the past?
“I was such-and-such a form in the past,” one feels delight therein; “I had such-and-such feeling...”
One takes delight in this: ‘In the past, I had such form’; one takes delight in this: ‘In the past, I had such perception’;
one takes delight in this: ‘In the past, I had such volitional formations’; one takes delight in this: ‘In the past, I had such consciousness.’
In this way, monks, one pursues the past.
And how, monks, does one not pursue the past?
One does not bring delight to the thought, "I was such-and-such a person in the past," nor does one bring delight to the thought, "I had such-and-such feelings..."
Regarding the past time, one does not take delight therein: "I had such a perception in the past," one does not take delight therein;
"I had such volitional formations in the past," one does not take delight therein;
"I had such consciousness in the past," one does not take delight therein.
In this way, monks, one does not pursue the past.
And how, monks, does one long for the future?
“May I be such-and-such a person in the future time”—thus one brings delight to that. “May I have such-and-such feeling” ... [and so on].

‘May I have such feeling in the future… may I have such volitional formations in the future… may I have such consciousness in the future,’ and one finds delight therein—it is in this way, monks, that one looks forward to the future.

And how, monks, does one not look forward to the future? [One thinks: ‘May I not have such feeling in the future… may I not have such volitional formations in the future… may I not have such consciousness in the future,’ and one does not find delight therein—it is in this way, monks, that one does not look forward to the future.
‘May I be such in form in the future,’ one does not take delight therein;
‘may I be such in feeling… may I be such in perception… may I be such in volitional formations… may I be such in consciousness in the future,’ one does not take delight therein.
In this way, monks, one does not long for the future.
And how, monks, is one carried away by present phenomena?

Here, monks, an uninstructed worldling—unseeing of the noble ones, unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, undisciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones; unseeing of true persons, unskilled in the Dhamma of true persons, undisciplined in the Dhamma of true persons—is carried away.
One regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as being in self, or self as being in form;
[and so with] feeling … perception … [etc.]

One regards volitional formations as self, or self as possessing volitional formations, or volitional formations as being in self, or self as being in volitional formations... One regards consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as being in self,
or self as being in consciousness— in this way, monks, one is drawn away from phenomena pertaining to the present.
And how, monks, is one not shaken regarding phenomena in the present?
Here, monks, the well-taught noble disciple—who has seen the noble ones, is skilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, and is well-disciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones;

who has seen true persons, is skilled in the Dhamma of true persons, and is well-disciplined in the Dhamma of true persons—does not regard form as self, nor self as possessing form, nor form as being in self, nor self as being in form.
not feeling … not perception … not volitional formations …
One does not regard consciousness as self, nor the self as possessing consciousness, nor consciousness as being in the self, nor the self as being in consciousness.
It is in this way, monks, that one is not shaken regarding present phenomena.
One should not pursue the past.
One should not long for the future;
for that which is past is abandoned,
and that which is yet to come has not been reached.
And whoever discerns, here and there, the phenomenon that has arisen,
as unshakable and unshakeable—
Knowing this, one should exert oneself:
"What must be done should be done with diligence today;
who knows if death will come tomorrow?"
For we have no compact with that Death who possesses a great army;
[we do not fear him] when one dwells thus, ardent.
"Unwearied day and night—
him indeed the peaceful Sage calls 'One Fortunate Night'."
“‘Monks, I will teach you the summary and the exposition of “One Who Has Had a Single Excellent Night.
It was with reference to this that it was said.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.
The First Discourse on the Single Excellent Night is finished.
